questions.question: A unit whole-life death benefit is paid at the end of the year of death. At current age $x$, first-year death probability is $q_x$, survival probability is $p_x=1-q_x$, and annual discount factor is $v>0$. Let $A_x$ be current APV and $A_{x+1}$ the next-age conditional remaining APV. In $A_x=vq_x+vp_xA_{x+1}$, what does $vq_x$ represent?
options: The issue APV contribution from surviving the first year.
The conditional benefit APV after surviving the first year.
The nominal benefit paid on every first-year outcome.
The issue APV contribution from death within the first year.

questions.question: For annual unit whole-life insurance, let $A_{x+1}$ be the benefit APV at age $x+1$ conditional on survival from age $x$. First-year survival probability is $p_x$ and annual discount factor is $v>0$. Which expression carries that continuation value back to age $x$ for every such survival probability, discount factor and continuation value?
options: $vq_xA_{x+1}$, where $q_x=1-p_x$

questions.question: In the annual whole-life recursion $A_x=vq_x+vp_xA_{x+1}$, let $p_x=1-q_x$ be strictly positive first-year survival probability and $v>0$ annual discount factor. Here $A_x$ is the current benefit APV. How should the next-age value $A_{x+1}$ be interpreted?
options: As the remaining contract value for those surviving to age $x+1$.
As a new policy value independent of first-year survival.
As the remaining value for policies that died before age $x+1$.
As the same mortality distribution as at age $x$ by definition.

questions.question: For annual unit endowment insurance, write $A_{x,n}$ for the APV of a contract with remaining term $n\ge0$ years. It pays at death within the term or at maturity otherwise. What terminal value is needed at $n=0$ for backward valuation?
options: $A_{x,0}=v$, where $v$ is the annual discount factor.
$A_{x,0}=q_x$, where $q_x$ is one-year death probability.

questions.question: For an annual-settlement unit death-only term insurance, write $D_{x,n}$ for APV with remaining term $n\ge0$. It pays only for death strictly before term expiry. What is the correct terminal value at zero remaining term?
options: $D_{x,0}=v$, where $v$ is annual discount factor.
$D_{x,0}=q_x$, where $q_x$ is first-year death probability.

questions.question: For annual unit whole-life insurance, annual discount factor is $v=0.9$, first-year death probability $q_x=0.1$, and next-age conditional APV $A_{x+1}=0.5$. What is the current-age APV $A_x$?

Annual unit whole-life insurance has $A_x=0.495$, annual discount factor $v=0.9$ and first-year death probability $q_x=0.1$. Its recursion is $A_x=v[q_x+(1-q_x)A_{x+1}]$. What is the next-age conditional APV?

For annual unit whole-life insurance, the insured is certain to die within the first year. The annual discount factor is $v=0.8$. Let $c$ be a formal finite continuation value for a survivor branch. What APV does first-year conditioning give?

A one-year unit endowment settles a death during the year at year end and otherwise pays the survival benefit at year 1. Annual discount factor is $v=0.9$ and first-year death probability is $q_x=0.2$. What does the endowment recursion give?

A one-year unit death-only term insurance pays at year end if death occurs during the year and nothing on survival. Annual discount factor is $v=0.9$ and death probability is $q_x=0.2$. What APV follows from the term recursion?

Let $A_{x,n}$ be annual-settlement unit endowment APV at age $x$ with integer remaining term $n\ge1$. Annual discount factor is $v>0$, and first-year probabilities are $q_x$ for death and $p_x=1-q_x$ for survival. Which recursion is valid for every such age, term and mortality basis?

An annual whole-life recursion uses current APV $A_x=vq_x+vp_xA_{x+1}$, with first-year death probability $q_x$, survival $p_x=1-q_x$, annual discount $0<v<1$ and conditional next-age APV $A_{x+1}$. An insurer changes death settlement from year end to the exact death instant. Why can the first-year death term not generally remain $vq_x$?
options: First-year death probability becomes the survival probability.
Deaths now have different first-year discount exponents.
The first-year death term loses every survival-related factor.
The continuation can no longer be conditional on surviving a year.

questions.question: In annual unit whole-life recursion, hold annual discount factor $0<v<1$ and next-age conditional APV $c$ fixed, with $0\le c<1$. Current APV at first-year death probability $q\in[0,1]$ is $A(q)=v[q+(1-q)c]$. Which formula gives its change for every such v,c when $q$ rises by $\Delta>0$ within the probability range?
options: $v(1-c)\Delta>0$
$vc\Delta>0$
$-v(1-c)\Delta<0$
$v\Delta$

questions.question: For annual unit whole-life insurance, annual discount factor is $v=0.9$ and first-year death probability is 0.2. Conditional on surviving that year, the remaining benefit PV at the next age is $W$, with $E[W]=0.4$ and $E[W^2]=0.25$. What is the second moment of the current benefit PV $Z$?

A two-year annual-settlement unit death-only term insurance has discount factor $v=0.9$, first-year death probability 0.2 and second-year death probability 0.4 conditional on survival. What is its issue APV under backward valuation?

An annual whole-life calculation uses discount factor $v=0.9$. Conditional first- and second-year survival probabilities are 0.8 and 0.7. The true remaining APV after two years is 0.5, but the numerical calculation sets that tail to zero and keeps all earlier death terms correct. How much does the issue APV fall?

A backward annual whole-life calculation sets the remaining benefit APV to zero at a chosen age $b$. Annual discount factors are positive. Survival to $b$ has positive probability, and the survivor basis gives positive probability of a later death benefit. What does that terminal choice do?
options: It gives exact whole-life value because the recursion itself is correct.
It adds a maturity benefit at age $b$ and overstates APV.
It changes only the value at $b$, leaving all earlier ages unchanged.
It omits positive remaining liability and understates the earlier APV.

questions.question: The annual recursion $A_x=v[q_x+(1-q_x)c]$ uses current APV $A_x$, discount factor $v>0$, first-year death probability $q_x$ and formal continuation value $c$. If $q_x=1$ and $A_x=v$, what can this equation tell us about $c$?
options: $c=0$ is the unique algebraic solution.
The equation leaves every finite $c$ possible.
$c=1$ is the unique algebraic solution.
$c=A_x/v=1$ follows by dividing out the discount.

questions.question: A proposed annual unit whole-life basis reports current APV $A_x=0.6$, next-age conditional APV $A_{x+1}=0.8$ and first-year death probability $q_x=0.1$. It claims one common annual discount factor $0<v<1$ for all future year-end unit payments. Is this basis consistent with the recursion and payment-value bounds?
options: Yes: $v=30/41$ lies between 0 and 1, so the recursion validates the basis.
No: recursion implies $v=0.75$, below the next-age APV.
No: recursion implies $v=30/41$, but $A_{x+1}=0.8>v$.
Yes: all reported APVs are below 1, so a common basis exists.

questions.question: At every integer age, annual survival is $p=0.8$ and death probability $q=0.2$, with discount factor $v=0.9$. The unit annual whole-life APV must satisfy $A_j=0.18+0.72A_{j+1}$, where $j\ge0$ indexes successive ages. A proposed sequence is $B_j=9/14+0.1(0.72)^{-j}$. Which assessment is correct?
options: It obeys the step but has an unjustified tail; true APV is $9/14$.
$B_j$ is the true APV because every one-year step equation holds.
$B_j$ fails the step equation, while the true APV is $9/14$.
$B_j$ obeys the step equation, so the true APV is only the first-year value 0.18.
